tasks.purpose: 分析社区食物浪费的原因和措施
tasks.setting: In some towns, households throw away large amounts of food that could still have been eaten. This increases the amount of waste that local authorities must collect and makes it harder for families to use their food budgets efficiently.
tasks.lead: What are the causes of this problem? What measures could be taken to address this problem?
bullets: Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
must: 分析家庭食物浪费的原因，并说明与原因对应的可行措施及其作用。
tasks.model:
Food that is bought but never eaten represents a loss to households and adds to the waste that towns have to manage. Much of this waste arises from purchasing more than people need and from uncertainty about storage. Retailers and local authorities can help families address both causes.

One reason for overbuying is that large packs or promotions appear cheaper than smaller quantities. A household may purchase more fresh produce than it can use simply to obtain a discount, only to discard part of it later. Busy people may also shop without checking what is already in their cupboards. As a result, they buy duplicate ingredients or make plans for meals that they do not have time to prepare.

Retailers could reduce the incentive to buy excessive amounts by offering smaller packs at a comparable price per unit. Customers would then be able to choose an appropriate quantity without paying a substantial premium. In addition, shops could provide simple shopping lists near fresh food displays, encouraging customers to plan meals and check supplies before their next visit. These measures would be most useful if families could still buy larger quantities when they genuinely needed them.

A second difficulty is that some people do not know how to keep food safely or how to use it before it deteriorates. Councils could distribute clear guidance on storage and suitable ways to use leftovers, for example through libraries and community centres. Practical demonstrations would be more useful than a general instruction to waste less, because residents could apply the advice to the food they routinely buy.

In conclusion, excess purchasing and uncertainty about storage can both contribute to household food waste. Smaller purchase options and accessible practical advice would tackle these causes directly, although their success depends on households choosing to use them.

tasks.purpose: 分析儿童步行上学减少的原因和措施
tasks.setting: In some urban neighbourhoods, fewer children walk to primary school than in the past, even when their homes are relatively close. More families use cars for these short journeys, contributing to congestion around school entrances.
tasks.lead: What are the causes of this problem? What measures could be taken to address this problem?
bullets: Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
must: 分析儿童较少步行上学的原因，并说明与原因对应的可行措施及其作用。
tasks.model:
Short journeys to primary school are increasingly made by car in some neighbourhoods. Parents may regard walking as unsafe or impractical within their daily routines. Safer routes and organised groups could make walking a realistic choice for more families.

Traffic itself can discourage parents from allowing children to walk. A route may involve crossing a busy road, and parked cars near the entrance can make it difficult for a small child to see approaching vehicles. Parents who must continue directly to work may also find it difficult to accompany a child on foot, particularly if the school route takes them away from their workplace. These concerns can reinforce one another: as more families drive, the area around the school can become still more congested.

Local authorities could respond to the first concern by improving crossings and restricting parking immediately outside school gates at arrival and departure times. A supervised crossing and a clear pavement would give children a safer place to approach the entrance. Such restrictions would need to be enforced and paired with a suitable drop-off point farther away; otherwise drivers might simply stop in another dangerous location.

Schools could also coordinate walking groups in which adults take turns accompanying children along an agreed route. This would allow parents who cannot walk with their children every morning to share the responsibility with other families. For example, a group could collect pupils at a local park and walk the final part of the journey together. The scheme would depend on sufficient volunteers and clear arrangements for supervision.

In conclusion, traffic risks and parents' schedules can make short car journeys seem necessary. Better crossings and shared supervision would address those barriers, making it easier for families to choose walking where the distance permits it.
